title: Hitler's Last 10 Days: Inside the Berlin Bunker
alt_titles: The Bunker: The Final Days of the Third Reich
What Really Happened in Hitler's Bunker
How the Hitler Escape Myth Was Finally Disproved
thumbnail_file: Ruins of the Reichstag in Berlin, 3 June 1945. BU8573.jpg
description_summary: In April 1945, as Soviet armies closed in on Berlin, Hitler spent his last days in a bunker beneath the Reich Chancellery. This is the story of those ten days, the collapse of the Nazi leadership, and how science finally disproved the escape myths.

scenes.narration: On the twentieth of April 1945, Adolf Hitler turned fifty six. He spent the day in a concrete bunker, deep beneath the centre of Berlin. That same day, Soviet artillery shelled the heart of the city for the first time. Above him, the capital was being destroyed street by street. Around him, his regime was falling apart. Ten days later, he was dead.

Nazi Germany had started a war that killed tens of millions of people. Its regime had murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. Now that regime was collapsing. In Berlin, civilians sheltered in cellars as the fighting drew near. Soviet armies were closing in from the east, and American and British forces from the west.

shots.file: File:Berlin- the Capture and Aftermath of War 1945-1947 BU8922.jpg
shots.caption: Berlin in ruins after the battle, 1945

scenes.narration: This is the story of those last ten days inside the bunker. It covers who was there and what happened. It also explains why myths about Hitler's fate refused to die for decades afterwards. It draws on witness accounts and later investigations.

shots.caption: Where the bunker lay, behind the Reich Chancellery

card.text: The last days of the Third Reich

shots.file: File:Ruins of the Reichstag in Berlin, 3 June 1945. BU8573.jpg
shots.caption: The ruined Reichstag, Berlin, June 1945

scenes.narration: The bunker lay under the garden of the old Reich Chancellery, Hitler's offices in Berlin. It had two levels. The lower one, the Führerbunker itself, was finished in 1944. It sat about eight and a half metres underground, under a roof of concrete nearly three metres thick.

shots.file: File:Ralph Reichhold - Map of the Führerbunker.jpg
shots.caption: A plan of the bunker's two levels

scenes.narration: Hitler moved in on the sixteenth of January 1945 and rarely left. The bunker sat below the water table, so pumps ran day and night. A diesel generator supplied the power. The air was damp, the rooms were cramped, and military conferences often ran until five in the morning.

By April, the bunker was crowded. Hitler's companion Eva Braun had joined him. So had his private secretary Martin Bormann, and propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels with his wife Magda and their six children. Two or three dozen staff worked there too, including secretaries, guards and a telephone operator.

shots.caption: Traudl Junge, one of Hitler's secretaries

scenes.narration: On the sixteenth of April, Soviet forces launched their final offensive. They crossed the River Oder and attacked the Seelow Heights, east of Berlin. German defenders held them for several days, at enormous cost to both sides. Then the line broke.

shots.caption: Soviet forces at the Seelow Heights, April 1945

scenes.narration: A month earlier, Hitler had made his last appearance in front of a newsreel camera. He met teenage members of the Hitler Youth in the Chancellery garden. Boys like these were now being sent to defend Berlin's streets.

shots.caption: Teenage Hitler Youth members in Berlin, 1945

scenes.narration: On the twenty first of April, Soviet tanks reached the edge of Berlin. Hitler ordered an SS general, Felix Steiner, to launch a counter-attack from the north. Steiner did not have the troops to do it. The attack never came.

stick.label: 21 April: tanks at the city's edge

scenes.narration: When Hitler learned the attack had not happened, he exploded with rage at his afternoon conference on the twenty second of April. For the first time, he said openly that the war was lost. He announced he would stay in Berlin, and die there.

card.text: Hitler admits the war is lost

scenes.narration: The next day, his armaments minister Albert Speer visited for the last time. A telegram also arrived from Hermann Göring, Hitler's designated successor, asking to take over the leadership of Germany. Bormann persuaded Hitler it was an attempted coup. Göring was stripped of his posts and arrested.

On the twenty eighth, a BBC report revealed that Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS, had secretly offered to surrender to the Western Allies. Hitler called it treason and ordered his arrest. Himmler's liaison in the bunker, Hermann Fegelein, who was married to Eva Braun's sister, was shot.

Around midnight on the night of the twenty eighth, Hitler married Eva Braun in a short civil ceremony in the bunker's map room. A local official was brought in to conduct it. A small wedding breakfast followed, as Soviet shells fell above.

Afterwards, he dictated his political testament to his secretary, Traudl Junge. He named Admiral Karl Dönitz as head of state and Goebbels as chancellor. Even now, he blamed the Jews for the war he had started. He signed it at four in the morning.

That afternoon, news reached the bunker that Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator and Hitler's ally, had been executed by Italian partisans. His body had been put on public display in Milan. Historians believe it strengthened his resolve not to be captured and put on display.

In the early hours of the thirtieth of April, Hitler said goodbye to his staff. That afternoon, at around half past three, he and Eva Braun took their own lives in his study. They had been married for less than two days.

card.label: Hitler and Eva Braun die in the bunker

scenes.narration: Following his orders, their bodies were carried up to the Chancellery garden, doused with petrol and burned. That evening, the remains were buried in a shallow shell crater. Inside the bunker, the remaining staff began planning their escape.

shots.file: File:Sergeant R S Baker of the Army Film & Photographic Unit (AFPU) looks at one of the giant chandeliers in the ruins of Hitler's Reich Chancellery in Berlin, 3 July 1945. BU8567.jpg
shots.caption: Inside the ruined Reich Chancellery, July 1945

card.text: The bodies are burned in the garden

scenes.narration: The next day, the German general Hans Krebs crossed the lines to tell the Soviets that Hitler was dead, and asked for a ceasefire. He was refused. That evening, Joseph and Magda Goebbels took their own lives. Before they died, their six children were poisoned in the bunker.

card.label: The Soviets learn of Hitler's death

scenes.narration: On the second of May, Berlin's garrison surrendered. Soviet troops captured the Reich Chancellery and the bunker. The last man to leave, an electrician named Johannes Hentschel, surrendered to the Red Army. He had stayed behind to keep the generators running.

card.label: Berlin surrenders
card.note: Twelve days after the birthday shelling

scenes.narration: Germany's armed forces surrendered unconditionally a few days later. The surrender was signed at Reims in France on the seventh of May, and came into force the next day. The eighth of May was celebrated as Victory in Europe Day.

shots.caption: Allied soldiers at the Brandenburg Gate, 1945

scenes.narration: That might have been the end of the story. But the Soviets kept what they had found secret. In early June, they said Hitler had died by poison. Days later, they said his body had not been identified and he had probably escaped. In July, Stalin claimed Hitler was living in Spain or Argentina. Later that year, a British intelligence officer, Hugh Trevor-Roper, investigated and concluded that Hitler had died in the bunker.

Those mixed messages fed a myth that has lasted for decades. Stories claimed Hitler slipped away by submarine to South America. Books and television documentaries repeated them. Historians who examined the claims found no credible evidence for any of them.

In fact, Soviet agents had recovered remains from the crater in 1945 and kept them in secret. In April 1970, the KGB dug them up, burned them again and scattered the ashes in a river. The aim was to make sure no grave could ever become a shrine.

card.label: How long the Soviets kept the remains secret

scenes.narration: Two pieces survived in Moscow archives: part of a skull and some teeth. In 2009, DNA tests suggested the skull fragment came from a woman, which revived the myths. Its origin had never been certain. But in 2017, a French team was allowed to examine the teeth, which had been held in Moscow since 1945. They matched Hitler's dental X-rays from 1944 perfectly.

Their study, published in 2018 in the European Journal of Internal Medicine, concluded that the remains could not be fake. Hitler had died in Berlin in 1945. Many researchers hoped it would finally end the escape theories. The science had confirmed what witnesses in the bunker had said all along.

card.label: Scientists confirm the teeth are Hitler's

scenes.narration: As for the bunker, the Soviets tried to blow it up in 1947, but only damaged the inner walls. East Germany demolished more of it from 1959. The site ended up close to the Berlin Wall, neglected, and most remaining sections were destroyed or filled in during the late 1980s.

card.text: The bunker is blown up and buried

scenes.narration: Today, the spot is an ordinary car park beside a block of flats, about three minutes' walk from Potsdamer Platz. A single information board was put up in 2006 to explain what once lay beneath. There is no memorial and nothing left to see.

shots.caption: The site of the bunker today
The site in 2007: a car park and housing

card.label: An information board marks the site

scenes.narration: Hitler died underground, his armies broken and his capital in ruins. The war in Europe ended eight days later. The war he started had cost tens of millions of lives. Sources and image credits are in the description.
